presentingComplaint: Fever and rigors with rapid deterioration 9 days after induction chemotherapy
history: Known acute myeloid leukaemia on day 9 of intensive induction chemotherapy (cytarabine + daunorubicin), managed via a tunnelled central venous catheter. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed painful oral ulceration limiting oral intake (grade 3 mucositis), then this evening spiked a fever to 39.4°C with drenching rigors. In the last 2 hours he has become clammy, confused and light-headed on standing. No localising urinary, respiratory or abdominal symptoms; no diarrhoea. No recent travel. He received no antibiotics in the preceding 90 days. Recorded penicillin 'rash' in childhood, subsequently tolerated cephalosporins without reaction.
examination: Toxic, mottled peripheries with prolonged capillary refill (4 s). Alert but disoriented to time. Oral cavity shows extensive ulcerative mucositis. Tunnelled line exit site is clean with no erythema or discharge; no fluctuance. Chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, no focal source identified. No rash, no meningism.

labs.map: 57 mmHg after 30 mL/kg crystalloid, requiring noradrenaline

imaging: Chest radiograph clear. Bedside echo shows hyperdynamic left ventricle with a collapsing IVC consistent with distributive shock; no pericardial effusion or vegetation seen.
microbiology: Two sets of paired peripheral and central-line blood cultures drawn before antibiotics; differential time-to-positivity requested. Urine culture and mucosal swabs sent. At 14 h, both peripheral and line cultures flag Gram-negative bacilli; at 40 h identified as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem and amikacin (not an ESBL/carbapenem-resistant phenotype). Differential time-to-positivity not suggestive of a line-primary source; no MRSA isolated.
differentialDiagnoses: Septic shock from an occult Gram-negative bacteraemia in a neutropenic host
Occult pneumonia / typhlitis as a source
Non-infective (drug/transfusion) pyrexia - excluded by shock and positive cultures
finalDiagnosis: High-risk febrile neutropenia (post-chemotherapy, ANC 120/uL) complicated by septic shock and acute organ dysfunction, source Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteraemia
citations: IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Use of Antimicrobial Agents in Neutropenic Patients with Cancer 2011
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Infections in Patients with Cancer
stewardship: High-risk febrile neutropenia (anticipated prolonged ANC <100, mucositis, haemodynamic instability) mandates immediate empiric anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy within one hour. Because the patient is in septic shock, guideline-concordant escalation adds an aminoglycoside (amikacin) for double Gram-negative cover and empiric vancomycin for the tunnelled line and severe mucositis; the childhood penicillin rash with tolerated cephalosporins does not preclude cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam. Once cultures confirm a fully susceptible, non-line-primary Pseudomonas aeruginosa and the patient stabilises, de-escalate to targeted anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime), stop vancomycin (no Gram-positive isolate) and stop the aminoglycoside once shock resolves. Continue until afebrile ≥48 h AND ANC recovering >500/uL.
contraindications: Avoid aminoglycoside continuation beyond shock resolution given evolving AKI (creatinine 1.9)
Nephrotoxin stacking (vancomycin + amikacin + contrast) requires level monitoring and renal dosing
Do not withhold empiric antibiotics to await imaging or a localising source
edgeCases: Persistent fever beyond 4-7 days despite broad cover should trigger empiric antifungal therapy and CT chest/sinuses
If cultures had shown carbapenem-resistant or ESBL organism, escalate to a carbapenem or novel beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor
Differential time-to-positivity favouring the line would mandate catheter removal for source control
expectedMaiK: Any fever in a patient with ANC <500/uL is a medical emergency requiring blood cultures and empiric broad-spectrum anti-pseudomonal antibiotics within one hour; with septic shock, escalate cover then de-escalate on culture data.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the current ANC and expected duration of neutropenia?
When did chemotherapy finish and what regimen was used?
Is there any catheter-site, respiratory, urinary, skin or perianal source?
Any prior resistant organisms, recent antibiotics or true beta-lactam allergy?
expectedInvestigations: Two sets of blood cultures (peripheral + central line) with differential time-to-positivity
Full blood count with differential (ANC), serum lactate, renal and liver profile, CRP/procalcitonin
Coagulation screen given thrombocytopenia and organ dysfunction

investigations: Paired peripheral and central-line blood cultures with differential time-to-positivity
FBC with ANC, lactate, renal and liver profile

regressionAssertions: Engine must identify high-risk febrile neutropenia (fever + ANC <500) as the primary diagnosis
Empiric therapy must include an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam started within one hour
Septic shock must trigger escalation (add aminoglycoside +/- vancomycin) then culture-directed de-escalation
Vancomycin and aminoglycoside must be stopped once no Gram-positive isolate and shock resolves
